title: Redwood structured output & function calling demo
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Aegis Financial through structured output and function-calling demo. Showed JSON mode, schema enforcement, guardrails for hallucination mitigation, and integrations with customer toolchain. Customer concerned about PII, KMS, VPC private deployment, and accuracy/loss from quantization. Agreed next steps: send security pack, pilot pricing, run a 24-hour benchmark with small dataset, schedule technical deep dive for infra team.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19 15:00 PT | Duration: 55m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Aegis CTO), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Samir (Infosec)

[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. we wanted to show a focused walkthrough on Redwood's structured output / function-calling flow — JSON mode, schema enforcement, and guardrails. Jordan will drive the demo.
[00:00:12] Jordan: yeah hi all, I'll share my screen. can you see the console?
[00:00:15] Carlos: yes, seeing it. audio's clear.
[00:00:20] Jordan: Great. quick context: Aegis asked about generating structured transaction enrichment payloads that feed into downstream workflows — so we want deterministic JSON outputs, strict schemas, and safe tool invocation so downstream systems don't break.
[00:00:35] Priya: that's right — we get inconsistent keys today, solves us a bunch of headaches during reconciliation. also concerned about hallucinations when the model invents a payment method or routing.
[00:00:45] Jordan: totally. so first i'll show JSON mode with an explicit JSON schema. here we have a schema for a transaction-enrichment object: fields like transaction_id, merchant_normalized, country_code, risk_score (0-100), routing_hint, confidence. and we run the model with function-calling style where the model returns a JSON matching the schema.
[00:01:10] [00:01:12] Jordan: launching an example request now — note the prompt includes schema and 'strict' guardrail flag.
[00:01:20] Maya: quick q from my side: Priya, is your team running on our hosted API or do you expect private deployment?
[00:01:27] Priya: for POC we're ok with hosted, but production will need VPC/private with our KMS and egress controls.
[00:01:33] Maya: great, good to know.
[00:01:35] Jordan: demo output: 
[00:01:40] {
  "transaction_id": "txn_12345",
  "merchant_normalized": "ACME-Mart",
  "country_code": "US",
  "risk_score": 42,
  "routing_hint": "use-gateway-3",
  "confidence": 0.87
}
[00:01:54] Priya: nice — that looks structured. a couple of things: 1) how do you guarantee types (we need ints not strings) and 2) what if the model refuses or returns an extra field?
[00:02:04] Jordan: good Q. the runtime enforces schema at two levels: pre-parse validation where we provide a JSON schema and the model is prompted to adhere; and runtime validation where Redwood will reject or attempt to repair outputs that don't conform. there are options: strict reject, auto-repair heuristics, or best-effort parse with confidence scoring.
[00:02:25] Samir: repair heuristics worry me from a security/audit perspective — we want deterministic behavior and an auditable trail.
[00:02:31] Jordan: understood — for enterprise we recommend strict mode with explicit failure paths and audit logs captured. the console shows the validation result, and every change is logged with the pre- and post- payload plus the confidence and model trace.
[00:02:45] [00:02:47] Jordan: i'll toggle strict mode to show rejection. re-run: output... model attempted to inject 'suggested_offer' but strict mode failed and returned a schema error. you can see the validation error in the console panel.
[00:03:02] Carlos: how do downstream systems get notified if a payload is rejected? do you have a DLQ or event stream?
[00:03:08] Maya: yes we have dead-letter queues, and you can route rejected outputs to a review queue or fallback static pipeline. Redwood rules let you configure per-route error handling — SNS, webhook, SQS, or write to S3 and trigger lambda.
[00:03:22] Priya: ok. what about function/tool calling — for example we want the model to call an enrichment microservice to fetch latest merchant metadata instead of hallucinating it.
[00:03:32] Jordan: perfect, watch this. I define a function with a typed interface: getMerchantData(merchant_id) returns merchant object. the model can emit a function call which we can either auto-execute or buffer for manual vetting.
[00:03:47] [00:03:50] Jordan: model chooses to call getMerchantData with payload {"merchant_id":"ACME-001"} — redwood runtime invokes the customer's endpoint via secure network path. note we support signed, short-lived credentials and mTLS for on-prem/VPC endpoints.
[00:04:06] Samir: so the runtime holds credentials? is that stored in your control plane? we need KMS/HSM separation.
[00:04:12] Jordan: we integrate with customer KMS and support HSM-backed keys for signing requests; for private deployments, the control plane can be air-gapped and the per-route secrets live in the customer's managed vault. for hosted we offer KMS integrations and token rotation.
[00:04:26] Carlos: good. latency wise, calling an external microservice on each token could kill p99s — how do you keep latency predictable?
[00:04:35] Jordan: we have a few levers: 1) we support prefetch/async calls — model can return a reference and we kick off enrichment async; 2) local caching via prefix/KV cache for merchant metadata; 3) dedicated pools for low-latency inference; 4) batched async requests for lower-cost high-throughput patterns.
[00:04:54] Priya: can you show caching?
[00:04:56] Jordan: sure — switching to the Optimize panel — here's a cache hit ratio dashboard. you can set TTLs and cache keys per-route. for merchant metadata TTL was set to 15m in this demo so most calls hit cache.
[00:05:12] [00:05:15] Jordan: also worth noting quantization/precision — if you're using 4-bit models to reduce cost, we recommend a small validation set to ensure structured fields (IDs, integers) aren't affected. Redwood Optimize will flag regressions on your eval sets.
[00:05:30] Priya: our worry: quantization might change the risk_score calibration. can we run a side-by-side?
[00:05:35] Maya: absolutely. typical pilot includes a 24-72 hour benchmark comparing hosted large-precision vs quantized dedicated profiles. we can run your transactions anonymized through the pipeline and produce token-level cost/latency and metric drift reports.
[00:05:49] Carlos: on compliance, we need SOC 2, ISO, and detailed audit logs. you mentioned audit trails earlier — can you show an example?
[00:05:56] Jordan: in the console here's an audit trace for a request: original prompt, model output, validation result, any repairs or function calls, and which key signed the call. we also capture operator actions — who re-ran or approved repairs. these logs are stored to a tenant-controlled S3 or sent to SIEM via webhook.
[00:06:15] Samir: and retention controls?
[00:06:18] Jordan: configurable retention per-tenant and per-route. for private deployments you can set retention to zero or to internal archive only.
[00:06:25] [00:06:27] Priya: practical question: our downstream engineers want deterministic mapping for merchant_normalized — can we supply a deterministic lookup table and let the model fallback only if no match?
[00:06:37] Jordan: yep — you can provide a ground-truth table as a retrieval layer. Redwood's routing supports hybrid approaches: call local DB first, then fall back to model, and the function-calling flow can prefer deterministic tooling. we'll show a quick sample where the model only proposes a 'probable_normalized' and we enrich it by merging with the lookup table in a follow-up function call.
[00:06:59] [00:07:02] Jordan: running that sample — model returns probable_normalized: "Acme Mart" with confidence 0.62, the runtime triggers getCanonicalMerchant which returns canonical "ACME-Mart" and we populate merchant_normalized with the canonical value. the whole exchange is recorded.
[00:07:20] Carlos: What about costs when you add function calls and routing — cost per token plus call cost?
[00:07:27] Maya: pricing can be per-token plus per-external-call if you use our managed function invocation (we bill minimal network hops). For dedicated customers we also offer reserved capacity discounts and can price pilots flat. we'll send an example pricing sheet.
[00:07:41] Priya: any limits on function schema complexity? We have nested merchant objects with lists of payment_methods.
[00:07:48] Jordan: JSON schema supports complex nested structures; function-calling can return nested objects, arrays. validation will ensure types and shapes. if you have extremely deep objects we recommend chunking or pre-defining subfunctions.
[00:08:03] [00:08:05] Maya: quick pause for clarifying timeline — what are your internal milestones for a POC?
[00:08:10] Carlos: we want a 4-week POC, prove correctness on 10k transactions, then decision for dedicated/private in Q3.
[00:08:18] Maya: great. we'll propose a POC plan.
[00:08:20] Jordan: back to demo — i'll show guardrails for hallucination: you can add 'deny-list' rules and rule-based sanity checks, e.g., risk_score must be between 0 and 100 and transaction_id must match regex ^txn_[0-9]+$. if a model violates that rule we can auto-correct or reject.
[00:08:40] Priya: can those rules be versioned? we need to roll back changes if something in production causes false positives.
[00:08:46] Jordan: yes config is versioned and tied to rollout policies — canary, A/B, or instant. you can test rules in a staging policy before promoting.
[00:08:56] Samir: for the data plane, is PII redaction supported? we want to ensure any raw inputs containing names or PAN don't persist.
[00:09:04] Jordan: Redwood supports redaction policies at ingestion: PII detectors and token scrubbing. plus customer-managed retention and ability to store only derived features. for private deployment you control data in your VPC.
[00:09:16] Carlos: ok, sounds promising. last thing: what would you need from us to start the POC?
[00:09:22] Maya: sample anonymized dataset (10k transactions), schema and lookup tables, list of success metrics (accuracy thresholds, max allowed drift), and point of contact for infra to set up either API keys or a test VPC endpoint.
[00:09:35] Carlos: we'll get that. Priya will own the dataset.
[00:09:39] Priya: yep.
[00:09:41] [00:09:43] Maya: wrap up — recap next steps in chat: we'll send pilot pricing, security pack (SOC2, ISO, KMS docs), and schedule a deep-dive with infra the week after next. Jordan will run a lightweight benchmark once we have the sample data.
[00:09:59] Carlos: thanks, appreciate it.
[00:10:02] Maya: thanks everyone.
[00:10:06] End of recorded transcript (note: transcript auto-generated; occasional mis-hearings expected).
